summary: Defines the format of the mailto URI scheme for identifying resources reached using internet mail. It improves internationalization and compatibility with IRIs over RFC 2368.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines the mailto: link, the one that opens a mail program with an address, a subject or a message body already filled in. It fixes which characters have to be escaped in such a link and how non-English characters are encoded, so that links written by one program work in another.

how do i put a subject in a mailto link
how to encode a space in a mailto link
subtitle: How a link can open a new email, with the recipient, subject and body already filled in.

tldr.problem: A web page often needs to point at a mailbox rather than at a document. The earlier mailto syntax, RFC 2368, was based on the older mailbox grammar and had no way to carry non-ASCII characters in a consistent way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives the mailto URI a syntax based on the RFC 5322 addr-spec, allows header fields after a question mark, and defines a body pseudo header field. Non-ASCII characters are encoded as UTF-8 and then percent-encoded, and a list of characters must be escaped.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6068 is a Proposed Standard from October 2010 that obsoletes RFC 2368. It also registers the Body header field name with IANA as reserved, so that no message header can clash with the mailto body field.

facts.label: Line break in a body field

today: RFC 6068 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2010. It obsoletes RFC 2368, so it is the definition of the mailto scheme, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The mailto URI scheme is used to identify resources that are reached using Internet mail. In its simplest form, a mailto URI contains an Internet mail address. For interactions that require message headers or message bodies to be specified, the scheme also allows mail header fields and the message body to be provided.

The specification extends the previous scheme definition of RFC 2368 to allow character data to be percent-encoded based on UTF-8, which offers a better and more consistent way of dealing with non-ASCII characters for internationalization. It does not address the needs of the ongoing Email Address Internationalization effort described in RFC 4952, and in particular it does not include syntax for fallback addresses.

In the document, URIs are enclosed in angle brackets as described in Appendix C of the URI generic syntax. Extra whitespace and line breaks are added to present long URIs and are not part of the actual URI.
sections.plainLanguage: A mailto link names a mailbox. It can also carry the fields of a message, such as the subject or the body, so that the person clicking the link gets a message already filled in. This version of the scheme adds a way to write non-English characters reliably.

sections.title: Syntax of a mailto URI
sections.content:
The syntax is written in Augmented Backus-Naur Form, using non-terminal definitions from the Internet Message Format, RFC 5322, for dot-atom-text and quoted-string, and from the URI generic syntax for unreserved and pct-encoded. The production is mailtoURI = "mailto:" [ to ] [ hfields ], where to is one or more comma-separated addr-specs and hfields is a question mark followed by header fields joined with ampersands.

The addr-spec is a mail address as specified in RFC 5322 but excluding the comment, with five changes. Characters that cannot appear in a URI, the percent sign itself, and the gen-delims except @ and : must be percent-encoded; of the sub-delims, at least &, ; and = must be percent-encoded as well, and care is needed so that encoding and decoding are each applied only once. The obs-local-part and NO-WS-CTL productions MUST NOT be used, and whitespace and comments within the local-part and domain MUST NOT be used, because they would have no operational semantics.

Percent-encoding can be used in the domain part to denote an internationalized domain name. Non-ASCII characters must first be encoded according to UTF-8 and then each octet must be percent-encoded. URI-producing applications MUST NOT use percent-encoding in domain names unless it is used to represent a UTF-8 character sequence, and when the name is used to compose a message it must be transformed to the IDNA encoding where appropriate. URI producers SHOULD provide these domain names in the IDNA encoding rather than percent-encoded, to maximize interoperability with legacy mailto interpreters.

Percent-encoding of non-ASCII octets in the local-part is reserved for the internationalization of the local-part; any other percent-encoding of non-ASCII characters is prohibited.

The header field names and values use the same escaping rules. The name is case-insensitive while the value is generally case-sensitive. The special header field name body indicates that its value is the body of the message, intended to hold the content of the first text/plain body part. It is meant for short text messages for automatic processing, such as subscribe messages for mailing lists, rather than for general MIME bodies. Apart from UTF-8 encoding and percent-encoding, no other encoding such as base64 or quoted-printable is used for the body field value, so header fields related to message encoding, such as Content-Transfer-Encoding, are irrelevant and MUST be ignored.

Within mailto URIs the characters ?, = and & are reserved as delimiters and have to be escaped as %3F, %3D and %26 when they are not serving as delimiters. Because the ampersand is also reserved in HTML and XML, a mailto URI containing one has to be written with an HTML or XML entity. It is syntactically valid to specify both an address and a header field named to, and the forms mailto:addr1@an.example,addr2@an.example, mailto:?to=addr1@an.example,addr2@an.example and mailto:addr1@an.example?to=addr2@an.example are equivalent, but the last is NOT RECOMMENDED because different user agents handle it differently and some ignore the to value. Implementations MUST NOT produce two To header fields in a message, and creators of mailto URIs SHOULD NOT use the same header field name more than once in the same URI. Fragment identifiers are meaningless in a mailto URI, SHOULD NOT be used, and SHOULD be ignored on resolution; the number sign in a header field value must be escaped as %23.
sections.plainLanguage: The link has two parts. Before the question mark is the address. After it are fields written as name and value, joined with ampersands, where the special name body means the message text. A few characters have a meaning of their own inside a link, so they must be escaped with a percent sign and two hex digits.

sections.title: Semantics and Operations
sections.content:
A mailto URI designates an Internet resource, which is the mailbox specified in the address. When additional header fields are supplied, the resource designated is the same address but with an additional profile for accessing it. While some Internet resources can only be accessed by electronic mail, the mailto URI is not intended as a way of retrieving such objects automatically.

The operation of how a URI scheme is resolved is not mandated by the URI specifications. Resolving an http URI causes an immediate interaction with a host running an interactive server. The mailto URI has unusual semantics, because resolving it does not cause an immediate interaction with a server. Instead, the client creates a message to the designated address with the various header fields set as default. The user can edit the message, send it unedited, or choose not to send it.

The header field names and values in a mailto URI, although syntactically equivalent to header fields in a mail message, do not directly correspond to them. In particular, the To, Cc and Bcc values do not necessarily result in a header field containing the specified value, because mail client software MAY eliminate duplicate addresses. Creators of mailto URIs SHOULD avoid using the same address twice.

Originator fields like From and Date, fields related to routing such as Apparently-To and the Resent fields, trace fields, and MIME header fields such as MIME-Version and Content-* MUST be ignored when present in the URI, and the mail client MUST create new fields when necessary, as it would for any new message. Unrecognized header fields, and header fields with values inconsistent with those the client would normally send, SHOULD be treated as especially suspect, although there may be header fields that are safe but unknown to the client, in which case the client MAY choose to show them to the user.

Section 4 of the RFC adds the rule for dangerous header fields: the user agent SHOULD NOT create a message if any of the header fields are considered dangerous, and it MAY choose to create a message with only a subset of the header fields given in the URI. A limited set of header fields such as Subject and Keywords, as well as Body, are believed to be both safe and useful in the general case. Where the source of a URI is well known, and specific header fields are limited to well-known values, other header fields MAY be considered safe too. The creator of a mailto URI cannot expect the resolver to understand more than the subject field and body, so clients that resolve mailto URIs into mail messages MUST be able to create RFC 5322-compliant messages using the subject header field and body.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening a mailto link does not send anything by itself. It opens a message with the fields filled in, and the person can change them or cancel. Some fields, such as the sender, the date and the routing fields, are ignored, because the mail program has to decide those for itself.

sections.title: Encoding
sections.content:
The URI generic syntax requires that many characters in URIs be encoded, which affects the mailto scheme for common characters that might appear in addresses, header fields or message contents. One such character is the space, which is written as %20. Line breaks in the body of a message MUST be encoded with %0D%0A. Implementations MAY add a final line break to the body of a message even if there is no trailing %0D%0A in the body field of the URI, and line breaks in other header fields SHOULD NOT be used.

When creating mailto URIs, any reserved characters that are used in them MUST be encoded so that properly written URI interpreters can read them. Client software that reads URIs MUST decode strings before creating the mail message, so that the message appears in a form the recipient's software will understand, and these strings SHOULD be decoded before the message is shown to the sending user.

Software creating mailto URIs likewise has to encode any reserved characters that are used. HTML forms are one kind of software that creates them, and current implementations encode a space as +. That creates problems, because such a plus standing for a space cannot be distinguished from a real plus in a mailto URI. When producing mailto URIs, all spaces SHOULD be encoded as %20, and plus characters MAY be encoded as %2B. Plus characters are frequently used as part of an email address to indicate a subaddress, as in bill+ietf@example.org.

The mailto scheme is limited in that it does not provide for substitution of variables. It is therefore impossible to create a mailto URI that includes a user's email address in the message body, and this limitation also prevents mailto URIs that are signed with public keys and other variable information.
sections.plainLanguage: A space in a link must be written as %20, not as a plus sign, because the plus sign can be a real plus in an address. A line break in the message body is written as %0D%0A. Because there is no way to substitute variables, a link cannot contain the reader's own address.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The basic examples cover the common cases. An ordinary individual address is mailto:chris@example.com. A mail response system that requires the name of the file to be sent back in the subject is mailto:infobot@example.com?subject=current-issue, and one that requires a send request in the body is mailto:infobot@example.com?body=send%20current-issue. A similar URI with two lines of send requests is mailto:infobot@example.com?body=send%20current-issue%0D%0Asend%20index.

When browsing archives of messages, a link can be provided that allows replying to a message and conserving threading information, by adding an In-Reply-To header field containing the Message-ID of the message where the link is added: mailto:list@example.org?In-Reply-To=%3C3469A91.D10AF4C@example.com%3E. A request to subscribe to a mailing list is mailto:majordomo@example.com?body=subscribe%20bamboo-l. A URI for a single user with a copy to another user is mailto:joe@example.com?cc=bob@example.com&body=hello, and the RFC notes that using a question mark twice, as in mailto:joe@example.com?cc=bob@example.com?body=hello, is wrong.

According to RFC 5322 the characters ?, & and even % may occur in addr-specs, and their being reserved characters is not a problem: they may appear in mailto URIs, just not in unencoded form. The address gorby%kremvax@example.com is written mailto:gorby%25kremvax@example.com, and the address unlikely?address@example.com with another header field is written mailto:unlikely%3Faddress@example.com?blat=foop. An address that itself includes an ampersand, such as Mike&family@example.org, is written mailto:Mike%26family@example.org.

Addresses with complicated escaping syntax are shown as well. The address "not@me"@example.org becomes mailto:%22not%40me%22@example.org, and the address "oh\no"@example.org becomes mailto:%22oh%5C%5Cno%22@example.org.

The UTF-8 examples show a subject of coffee in French, written with the final e as an e-acute: mailto:user@example.org?subject=caf%C3%A9. The same subject written as an encoded word, with the equals sign and question mark of the encoded-word syntax escaped because they are reserved, is mailto:user@example.org?subject=%3D%3Futf-8%3FQ%3Fcaf%3DC3%3DA9%3F%3D, and the same subject encoded as iso-8859-1 is mailto:user@example.org?subject=%3D%3Fiso-8859-1%3FQ%3Fcaf%3DE9%3F%3D. Adding a body with the same value gives mailto:user@example.org?subject=caf%C3%A9&body=caf%C3%A9, which may result in a message with the subject =?utf-8?Q?caf=C3=A9?= and the body caf=C3=A9. The final example uses the Japanese word natto, Unicode characters U+7D0D U+8C46, as a domain name label: mailto:user@%E7%B4%8D%E8%B1%86.example.org?subject=Test&body=NATTO. When constructing the email, the domain name label is converted to punycode, so the message may show the address as user@xn--99zt52a.example.org.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples cover a plain address, a subject, a body, a copy to someone else, and addresses with unusual characters in them. They also show a Japanese domain name, which is written percent-encoded in the link and turned into punycode when the message is built.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mailto scheme can be used to send a message from one user to another, and thus introduces many security concerns. Mail messages can be logged at the originating site, the recipient site and intermediary sites along the delivery path, and if the messages are not encrypted they can be read at any of those sites.

A mailto URI gives a template for a message that can be sent by mail client software. The contents of that template may be opaque or difficult to read by the user when the URI is specified, and they may be hidden in the user interface, for example when a link on an HTML page displays something other than the content of the URI that would be used when it is clicked. A mail client SHOULD therefore NOT send a message based on a mailto URI without first disclosing and showing to the user the full message that will be sent, including all header fields specified by the URI, fully decoded, and asking the user to approve sending it as electronic mail. The client SHOULD also make it clear that the user is about to send an electronic mail message, since the user may not be aware that this is the result of a mailto URI, and users are strongly encouraged to check that the URI presented to them matches the address in the To line of the message.

Some header fields are inherently unsafe to include in a message generated from a URI. In general, the fewer header fields interpreted from the URI, the less likely it is that a sending agent will create an unsafe message. The RFC lists examples of problems with sending unapproved mail: mail that breaks laws upon delivery, such as making illegal threats; mail that identifies the sender as someone interested in breaking laws; mail that identifies the sender to an unwanted third party; mail that causes a financial charge to be incurred by the sender; and mail that causes an action on the recipient's machine that causes damage that might be attributed to the sender. Programs that interpret mailto URIs SHOULD ensure that the SMTP envelope return path address, given as the argument to the MAIL FROM command, is set and correct, and that the resulting email is a complete, workable message.

Mailto URIs on public web pages expose mail addresses for harvesting. This applies to all mail addresses that are part of the URI, including the addresses in a bcc value. Those addresses are not sent to the recipients in the to field or in the to and cc values, but they are still publicly visible in the URI, and they may also leak to other addresses in the same value or become known otherwise, depending on the mail user agent used.

Programs manipulating mailto URIs have to take great care not to double-escape or double-unescape them, and to make sure that escaping and unescaping conventions relating to URIs and to mail addresses are applied in the right order. Implementations parsing mailto URIs must sanity check them in order to avoid buffer overflows and problems resulting from them, such as the execution of code specified by the attacker. The security considerations of the URI generic syntax, RFC 5890, RFC 5891 and RFC 3987 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can hide what it will do, so the mail program should show the whole message and ask before sending it. A link on a public page also shows the addresses in it to everyone, including any hidden copy address, so those addresses can be collected for unwanted mail.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This document changes the definition of the mailto URI scheme, and the registry of URI schemes has been updated to refer to this document rather than its predecessor, RFC 2368. The registration template gives the scheme name as mailto, the status as permanent, the syntax and semantics as the sections of this document, and the encoding considerations as the syntax and encoding sections. The applications that use this scheme name are noted as being widely used since the start of the Web. The interoperability considerations record that interoperability for mailto URIs with UTF-8-based percent-encoding might be somewhat lower than interoperability for mailto URIs with US-ASCII only. The contact and the author and change controller are both the IETF.

IANA has registered the Body header field in the Message Header Fields Registry, RFC 3864, with the applicable protocol listed as None, because the registration is made to assure that this header field name is not used at all, in order not to create any problems for mailto URIs. Its status is reserved and its specification document is RFC 6068.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme is registered with IANA under this document rather than the older one, and the header field name Body is reserved so that no mail program can use it for something else and confuse a mailto link.

sections.title: Main Changes from RFC 2368
sections.content: The main changes from RFC 2368 are a change of syntax from the RFC 2822 mailbox production to the RFC 5322 addr-spec; the allowance of UTF-8-based percent-encoding for domain names and in header field values; a tightening of percent-encoding in the local-part to be based on UTF-8, reserved for if and when there is a specification for the internationalization of email addresses; the removal of the prohibition against Bcc header fields, together with a warning about their visibility and harvesting for spam; and added clarifications for escaping.
sections.plainLanguage: Compared with the older version, the address grammar follows the current mail format, non-English text can be written directly, and a hidden copy address is allowed, with a warning that it stays visible in the link.

viz.caption: THE SYNTAX OF A mailto URI, AS GIVEN IN RFC 6068 SECTION 2

data.title: mailto URI syntax
data.code:
mailtoURI    = "mailto:" [ to ] [ hfields ]
to           = addr-spec *("," addr-spec )
hfields      = "?" hfield *( "&" hfield )
hfield       = hfname "=" hfvalue
hfname       = *qchar
hfvalue      = *qchar
addr-spec    = local-part "@" domain
local-part   = dot-atom-text / quoted-string
domain       = dot-atom-text / "[" *dtext-no-obs "]"
dtext-no-obs = %d33-90 / %d94-126
qchar        = unreserved / pct-encoded / some-delims
some-delims  = "!" / "$" / "'" / "(" / ")" / "*"
             / "+" / "," / ";" / ":" / "@"

viz.caption: WHAT A MAIL CLIENT DOES WITH EACH KIND OF HEADER FIELD IN A LINK

columns: What the client does with it

cells: Used as defaults, but the client may remove duplicate addresses, so the value does not have to appear as given
Believed to be safe and useful in the general case
From, Date, Apparently-To, Resent-*, trace fields, MIME-Version, Content-*
MUST be ignored; the client creates its own values
Unrecognized fields, or fields with odd values

viz.caption: HOW COMMON CHARACTERS ARE WRITTEN INSIDE A mailto LINK

items.title: Space
items.text: Written as %20. A plus sign should not be used, because it may be a real plus in the address.

items.title: Line break
items.text: Written as %0D%0A in the body field.

items.title: Question mark
items.text: Written as %3F when it is not the delimiter that starts the header fields.

items.title: Equals sign
items.text: Written as %3D when it is not the delimiter between a field name and its value.

items.title: Ampersand
items.text: Written as %26 inside an address, and as & in HTML or XML.

items.title: Number sign
items.text: Written as %23 inside a header field value.

items.title: Percent sign
items.text: Written as %25, because it introduces an escape.

items.title: Plus sign
items.text: May be written as %2B. A plus often marks a subaddress.
